claim.precise: Psalm 22:14–15 predicted Jesus's agony on Calvary, fulfilled in Mark 15:34–37.
claim.scope_notes: Mark explicitly quotes Psalm 22:1 in this scene, but the proposed prediction is the general fact of extreme suffering.

context.summary: Psalm 22 vividly describes a sufferer physically failing and approaching death. Mark depicts Jesus crying out, receiving sour wine and dying on the cross.

strongest_case.summary: Mark places Jesus's quotation of Psalm 22:1 directly inside the crucifixion account. The psalm's bodily collapse, dry mouth and nearness to death give a powerful script for understanding Jesus's final agony.
reasoning: Jesus quotes the psalm's opening line in Mark.
Both passages portray intense suffering near death.
The sour wine also fits the dry-mouth setting.

critical_case.summary: ‘Suffered agony’ is not a distinctive prediction: countless people have experienced pain and death. The psalm is a present-tense lament, and Mark's explicit quotation shows literary interpretation without proving that verses 14–15 forecast Calvary.
reasoning: Agony is too general to identify Jesus.
The psalm describes a current sufferer.
Literary reuse is not the same as advance prediction.

verdict.summary: Mark clearly invites readers to view Jesus through Psalm 22. That is a strong interpretive connection, but ‘a sufferer experiences agony’ is too general to work as a specific prediction of Calvary.

objections.objection: The draft tests whether agony uniquely identifies Jesus, while a proponent may offer it cumulatively.
objections.reason: The verdict is limited to this item as a specific prediction and does not reject a cumulative Christian reading.

objections.objection: A present-tense lament can still have typological or prospective significance.
objections.reason: The copy says the passage is not an obvious forecast rather than excluding additional theological meaning.

objections.objection: Literary reuse and fulfilment are not mutually exclusive.
objections.reason: The final assessment affirms Mark's real interpretive connection and only denies that reuse alone proves advance prediction.

publication_copy.title: Agony at Calvary
publication_copy.scripture_excerpt: My strength is dried up … You lay me in the dust of death.

website.description: Did Psalm 22 predict Jesus's agony on the cross?
website.summary: Mark deliberately connects Jesus with Psalm 22, but extreme suffering is not a specific identifying prediction.
website.christian_case: Jesus quotes the psalm's opening from the cross. The later images of bodily collapse, thirst and approaching death closely fit his final moments.
website.critical_case: The connection is real, but ‘he would suffer terribly’ could fit many people. The psalm speaks as a sufferer in his own crisis, not as an obvious forecast of Calvary.
website.verdict_label: A later reading of the psalm
website.verdict: Mark uses Psalm 22 to interpret Jesus's death. That does not make its general picture of agony a precise prediction.

carousel.heading: Did Psalm 22 predict Calvary’s agony?
carousel.body: The psalm describes a body failing near death. Mark describes Jesus crying out and dying on the cross.

carousel.heading: Mark makes a real connection
carousel.body: Jesus quotes the opening of Psalm 22. Readers are clearly meant to see his death through this ancient lament.

carousel.heading: But agony is not very specific
carousel.body: Many people suffer terribly before death. The psalm fits Jesus, but it does not uniquely predict Calvary.
